questions.q: The viral vector that delivers genes into cells; the CRISPR Cas9 coding sequence has to be delivered into the cell before it can act, and Cas9 is short enough to fit inside a vector — what is this vector called?
questions.why: adenovirus is the viral vector that delivers genes into cells; he does not name it as a question in its own right — the point of the same passage is that 'Cas9 is short enough to fit inside a vector'.

questions.q: Inflammation is not only about starting up, it has to be able to shut down as well, otherwise the body stays on permanent alert: the class of molecules that switches inflammation off once the threat has passed is called ______.
questions.why: An anti-inflammatory mediator is the class of molecule that switches inflammation off once the threat has passed; it is the closing point of the NF-κB passage in lecture five, and he explicitly said that the order of the cytokines does not have to be memorised.

questions.q: In the multi-step pathway of colorectal cancer, APC is the first brake to fail. What does it normally do?
options: In the liver, it turns drugs and toxins into more reactive molecules
It converts AMP into adenosine, making the area around the tumour immunosuppressive
It carries the ITAM and passes the CAR signal on to ZAP-70
It inhibits Wnt signalling and holds down beta-catenin, stopping cells from dividing endlessly
questions.why: APC is an inhibitory protein of the Wnt signalling pathway that under normal conditions holds down beta-catenin; it is the first brake gene to fail in the multi-step colorectal cancer pathway, while the distinction between driver and passenger is what he marks as Tier 2.

questions.q: The aristolochic acid of Chinese herbal medicine, one of the four carcinogens he lists; like the tobacco carcinogens it has to be metabolically activated before it can damage DNA — what is this carcinogen called?
questions.why: aristolochic acid I (AA-I) is the aristolochic acid of Chinese herbal medicine and one of the four carcinogens he lists; he never asks you to memorise a list of carcinogens — what has to stay in your head is the chain 'carcinogen → adduct → replication error → fixed as a mutation'.

questions.q: In lecture three, when he covers chemical carcinogenesis, he says the nitrosamines in tobacco are not directly carcinogenic themselves: after activation by liver P450, the activated carcinogenic precursor adds an aromatic amine group to a DNA base — what is this chemical step called?
questions.why: Arylamination is the chemical step in which the activated carcinogenic precursor adds an aromatic amine group to a DNA base; once a DNA adduct has formed, if it is not repaired, the second round of replication fixes it into a mutation.

questions.q: His checkpoint slide in lecture three splits checkpoint inhibitors into two columns: anti-PD-1 covers pembrolizumab and nivolumab, while anti-PD-L1 includes atezolizumab, durvalumab and avelumab. What is the first drug in the anti-PD-L1 column called?
questions.why: Atezolizumab is the immune checkpoint inhibitor that targets PD-L1; he does not single out this drug name as a question in its own right — what is actually named is the concept of hot versus cold tumour and the response of MSI-H to anti-PD-1.

questions.q: A tobacco carcinogen that, after activation in the cell, forms an adduct with DNA; if the adduct is not repaired, the second round of replication fixes it into a mutation — what is this carcinogen called?
questions.why: Benzo(a)pyrene is a tobacco carcinogen that forms an adduct with DNA after activation in the cell; how an unrepaired adduct becomes fixed as a mutation is the point of this passage, and he did not list benzo(a)pyrene on its own as a question.

questions.q: In lecture three he introduces CAR-NK and CAR-macrophages to show that 'CAR-T is not the only solution': putting the CAR on a natural killer cell rather than on a T cell — what is this approach called?
questions.why: CAR-NK is putting the CAR on a natural killer cell rather than on a T cell; he uses CAR-NK and CAR-macrophages to show that CAR-T is not the only solution, which belongs to conceptual understanding.

questions.q: The role that comes up most often when reading a pedigree: carrying one faulty copy of a gene without showing the disease yourself. What is such a person called?
questions.why: A carrier is someone who carries one faulty copy of a gene without showing the disease; pedigree reading and carrier probability are the scenario questions he named explicitly (case bank number 2).

questions.q: The covalently closed circular DNA that HBV forms in the nucleus; it acts as a persistent episomal reservoir inside the nucleus, which is why HBV is so hard to eradicate — what is this molecule called?
questions.why: cccDNA is the covalently closed circular DNA that HBV forms in the nucleus; it is a persistent episomal reservoir inside the nucleus, which is why the virus is so hard to eradicate, and he drew HBV's full life cycle on slide 17.

questions.q: The chemokine receptor that lets monocytes follow the CCL2/MCP-1 signal to find the tumour; he lists it together with CCR4 among the missing receptors on the solid-tumour barriers list — what is this receptor called?
questions.why: CCR2b is the chemokine receptor that lets monocytes follow the CCL2/MCP-1 signal to find the tumour; he does not single it out as a question in its own right — the 'solid-tumour barriers' list is the backbone of this passage.

questions.q: In lecture two he lists the obstacles that make CAR-T fail in solid tumours, among them the absence of chemokine receptors: CCR2b recognises CCL2/MCP-1, and which other receptor recognises CCL17?
questions.why: CCR4 is the chemokine receptor that recognises CCL17 and, like CCR2b, belongs to the missing receptors on his list; he did not name it specifically, so it is conceptual understanding.

questions.q: The signalling subunit of the T-cell receptor complex, with no recognition function of its own but carrying the ITAM motif; the CAR uses it as its final segment, just as the scFv is the microphone and this is the loudspeaker — this intracellular signalling domain is called ______.
questions.why: CD3ζ is the signalling subunit of the T-cell receptor complex; it carries the ITAM motif and passes the signal to ZAP-70. The CAR uses it as its final segment, which is like borrowing the 'answer button' of a mobile phone, and he did not list it as a question on its own.

questions.q: In lecture two he uses two molecules to explain how a tumour makes the immune system back off: CD47 and CD73 each do one thing. Which of the following pairings is correct?
options: CD47 makes phagocytes back off, while CD73 converts AMP into adenosine
CD47 converts AMP into adenosine, while CD73 makes phagocytes back off
Both of them are chemokine receptors
Both of them are signals that activate T cells
questions.why: CD47 is the 'do not eat me' signal on the tumour surface that makes phagocytes back off; CD73 is the enzyme that converts AMP into adenosine, making the area around the tumour immunosuppressive. He lists CD47 among the hostile physical environment, so it is conceptual understanding.

questions.q: Among the hostile physical environment of lecture two there is an enzyme that converts AMP into adenosine, making the area around the tumour immunosuppressive — what is this enzyme called?
questions.why: CD73 is the enzyme that converts AMP into adenosine, making the area around the tumour immunosuppressive; he did not name it specifically, so it is conceptual understanding.

questions.q: He says this is basic biochemistry background that lecture one did not expand on: the small helper molecule that an enzyme needs while it works is called ______.
questions.why: A coenzyme is the small helper molecule an enzyme needs while it works; he did not expand on it in lecture one, but he did say explicitly that chemical structures and metabolic details do not have to be memorised, so it is conceptual understanding.

questions.q: He says this is basic biochemistry background that lecture one did not expand on: the partner an enzyme needs that is not itself a protein, often a metal ion, is called ______.
questions.why: A cofactor is the partner an enzyme needs that is not itself a protein, often a metal ion; he says explicitly that chemical structures and metabolic details do not have to be memorised, so it is conceptual understanding.

questions.q: When a set of similar DNA sequences is compared, people take the base that occurs most frequently as the representative; what is this 'representative letter' concept called?
questions.why: A consensus sequence is the DNA 'letter' that occurs most frequently in a real genome; he did not list it as a question, so it is conceptual understanding.

questions.q: The specialist scavenger among immune cells, picking up antigens and displaying them for T cells to inspect; it supplies co-stimulation, which is the prerequisite for understanding anergy and T-cell activation — what is this cell called?
questions.why: A dendritic cell is the specialist scavenger among immune cells, picking up antigens and displaying them for T cells to inspect; this role of providing co-stimulation is the prerequisite for understanding anergy and T-cell activation.

questions.q: The molecules that keep poorly soluble membrane proteins in shape in water; they are neither receptors nor enzymes, yet they are an indispensable chemical aid when studying membrane proteins — what are such molecules called?
questions.why: Detergents are the molecules that keep poorly soluble membrane proteins in shape in water; he did not single them out as a question in their own right, so it is conceptual understanding.

questions.q: HBV's cccDNA is a persistent episomal reservoir in the nucleus, which is why HBV is so hard to eradicate. Which statement about the relationship between episome, cccDNA and rcDNA is correct?
options: The three are in fact three different names for the same molecule
An episome always integrates into the host chromosome, whereas cccDNA and rcDNA never do

cccDNA is the covalently closed circular DNA formed in the nucleus, rcDNA is the relaxed circular DNA that exists before entry into the nucleus, and an episome is DNA that is not part of the host chromosome and can replicate independently
rcDNA is the DNA adduct formed after P450 has activated a carcinogen
questions.why: An episome is a DNA molecule that is not part of the host chromosome and can replicate independently; he did explain the mechanism that 'HBV cccDNA is a persistent episomal reservoir in the nucleus, and therefore hard to eradicate', and he drew HBV's full life cycle on slide 17.

questions.q: In lecture three, when he covers the molecular mechanisms of CNV, he says 'I am only giving you a taste, do not be frightened by these mechanisms', but one of the replication pathways is fork stalling and template switching — what is that pathway called?
questions.why: FoSTeS is fork stalling and template switching, the replication pathway that generates CNVs; he states clearly that the molecular mechanisms of CNV are not examined, but what NAHR is, and the concept of adaptive CNV, still fall within the range of understanding.

questions.q: A large family of membrane receptors, which he calls the best drug target; it appears on both of the threads 'membrane proteins are the primary drug targets' and Hippo signal transduction — what is this family of receptors called?
questions.why: GPCRs are a large family of membrane receptors and the best drug targets; they are the entry point for understanding his 'receptor → kinase cascade' logic, and belong to conceptual understanding.

questions.q: When teaching the basics of flow cytometry he says: FSC is size, SSC is granularity, and the population of cells with high SSC is precisely the granulocytes — what is this population of cells called?
questions.why: Granulocytes are the cells occupying the high side scatter region of a flow plot; he did not single them out as a question in their own right — gating and the meaning of SSC are what he marks as Tier 2.

questions.q: He says this term is not in the content of his five lectures and belongs to background knowledge, but he asks you not to confuse it with the other kinds of recombination. Which of the following pairings is correct?
options: The two are in fact the same thing, merely described differently
Homoeologous recombination is an explicitly listed question in his five lectures

Homoeologous recombination is recombination between similar but not fully homologous chromosomes, the mechanism behind breeding polyploid crops, whereas NAHR is recombination between two similar but not identical stretches of DNA, which causes chromosomal rearrangement
Both of them necessarily cause chromosomal rearrangement
questions.why: Homoeologous recombination is recombination occurring between similar but not fully homologous chromosomes; he neither names it nor excludes it, and all you have to do is not to confuse it with NAHR and human homologous recombination.

questions.q: In lecture two, when he discusses the matrix of the tumour microenvironment, he mentions a class of negatively charged macromolecules: heparan sulfate proteoglycans, listed on the solid-tumour barriers list — what are such macromolecules called?
questions.why: HSPGs are heparan sulfate proteoglycans, the negatively charged macromolecules of the tumour matrix; he did not name them specifically — the TME list itself is the point.

questions.q: A cell-surface protein that grips other cells and the matrix; leukocytes hold on with it as they move, and it is also an example of the proposition that 'membrane proteins are the primary drug targets' — what is this protein called?
questions.why: Integrin is a cell-surface protein that grips other cells and the matrix, and leukocytes hold on with it as they move; it appears on his four-step leukocyte extravasation diagram and is also an example of the proposition that 'membrane proteins are the primary drug targets'.

questions.q: Channels embedded in the cell membrane that let ions move in and out down their concentration gradients; his view that 'receptors on the membrane are easier to make drugs against than intracellular targets' is built on them — what is this membrane channel called?
questions.why: Ion channels are channels embedded in the cell membrane that let ions move in and out down their concentration gradients; he did not single them out as a question in their own right, but 'receptors on the membrane are easier to make drugs against than intracellular targets' is a view from chapter 6.

questions.q: On his checkpoint slide in lecture three, besides anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 there is a third brake, CTLA-4; what is the drug that works by releasing the T-cell brake called?
questions.why: Ipilimumab is an anti-CTLA-4 checkpoint inhibitor whose action is to release the T-cell brake; he expects you to state the difference in where the CTLA-4 and PD-1 brakes sit and which drug corresponds to each.

questions.q: The proteins located at cell junctions that recruit and switch on the Hippo kinases; when reviewing Hippo in lecture five he points out that cell contact is the entry point for switching Hippo on, and that Hippo being off is cancer — these three proteins are ______.
questions.why: KIBRA, MER and WILLIN sit at cell junctions and are responsible for recruiting and switching on the Hippo kinases; he points out that cell contact is the entry point for switching Hippo on and that Hippo being off is cancer, and these three proteins are the first stop on his slide.

questions.q: In lecture three, when he covers the molecular mechanisms of CNV, he does not demand a deep dive, but among them he mentions the mechanism of transposable element insertion, which in English is mobile element insertion — what is this mechanism called?
questions.why: MEI is mobile element insertion, the CNV-generating mechanism caused by insertion of a transposable element; he states clearly that the molecular mechanisms of CNV are not examined, but he did cover the two concepts NAHR and adaptive CNV.

questions.q: When teaching flow cytometry he says: granulocytes occupy the high side scatter region, while monocytes sit between the granulocytes and the lymphocytes on the flow plot — what is this population of cells called?
questions.why: Monocytes are the cells that sit between the granulocytes and the lymphocytes on a flow plot; he did not single out monocytes as a question in their own right, so it is conceptual understanding.

questions.q: Anything that causes mutations, for example a chemical or some form of radiation; he uses the chain 'adduct → replication error → fixed as a mutation' to explain carcinogenesis and lists examples such as NNK and 4-aminobiphenyl — what is this class of things collectively called?
questions.why: A mutagen is anything that causes mutations, for example a chemical or some form of radiation; he lists examples such as NNK and 4-aminobiphenyl, but he does not ask you to memorise the list.

questions.q: In lecture three, when he covers the mechanisms of CNV, he says this part is only 'just a taste' and does not require a deep dive; but the duplication and deletion produced by NAHR remain the standard explanation for CNV. Why must NAHR and homoeologous recombination not be confused with each other?
options: NAHR is recombination between two similar but not identical stretches of DNA and causes chromosomal rearrangement, whereas homoeologous recombination is recombination between similar but not fully homologous chromosomes and is the mechanism behind breeding polyploid crops
The two are completely identical, merely described differently
NAHR occurs only in bacteria and homoeologous recombination only in humans
NAHR necessarily causes cancer whereas homoeologous recombination does not
questions.why: NAHR is recombination between two similar but not identical stretches of DNA, which causes chromosomal rearrangement; he says explicitly that this part is only 'just a taste' and does not require a deep dive, but the duplication and deletion produced by NAHR are the standard explanation for CNV.

questions.q: His checkpoint slide in lecture three lists anti-PD-1 as two drugs: pembrolizumab and this one — what is that drug called?
questions.why: Nivolumab is an anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor; he lists anti-PD-1 as pembrolizumab and nivolumab and anti-PD-L1 as atezolizumab, durvalumab and avelumab, and this set of drug names paired with the MSI-H indication is a common combination in scenario questions.

questions.q: One of the tobacco-specific nitrosamines, which is activated by liver P450 before it binds DNA; his slide records that it causes a GC→AT mutation in K-ras in mice — what is this nitrosamine called?
questions.why: NNK is one of the tobacco-specific nitrosamines and is activated by liver P450 before it binds DNA; he wrote 'NNK induces a GC→AT mutation in the K-ras gene in mice' on the slide, but he did not ask you to memorise the detailed chemical steps of carcinogens.

questions.q: He named two molecules among the tobacco-specific nitrosamines; the one other than NNK is called ______.
questions.why: NNN is the other tobacco-specific nitrosamine; he did not ask you to memorise the names — what matters in this passage is that 'if the adduct is repaired nothing happens, and if it is not repaired it becomes a permanent mutation'.

questions.q: A small human tissue section grown from stem cells and used for drug testing; in lecture two he draws it as one step on the drug R&D route of 'directed differentiation into an organoid → multiwell plate drug screening → activity readout → target validation' — what is this model called?
questions.why: An organoid is a small human tissue section grown from stem cells and used for drug testing; he places it on the drug R&D route of 'directed differentiation → multiwell plate drug screening → activity readout → target validation'.

questions.q: The place in the cytoplasm where silenced mRNA is gathered up and destroyed; on his lecture-five diagram of miRNA biogenesis he places the site of action of RISC and GW182 here — what is this place called?
questions.why: A P-body is the place in the cytoplasm where silenced mRNA is gathered up and destroyed; on the same diagram he also explains that miRNA is unusually stable in serum, which makes it suitable as a non-invasive biomarker.

questions.q: Cytochrome P450, the family of enzymes in the liver that turn drugs and toxins into more reactive molecules; the sequence that 'a toxin must be metabolised before it damages DNA' depends on it — what is this enzyme family called?
questions.why: P450 is cytochrome P450, the family of liver enzymes that turn drugs and toxins into more reactive molecules; he did not name it on its own, but the sequence that 'a toxin must be metabolised before it damages DNA' is the key point.

questions.q: In lecture four he cites the study by Le DT and colleagues: the progression-free survival curve of dMMR versus pMMR (P<0.001 by log-rank test), which he calls 'one of the most important figures in modern medicine'; the anti-PD-1 drug used is this one — what is this drug called?
questions.why: Pembrolizumab is an anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitor and the drug for hot tumours such as MSI-high; he cites the study by Le DT and colleagues and calls that figure 'one of the most important figures in modern medicine'.

questions.q: A signalling enzyme that can switch on inflammatory and growth pathways; he marks it on both the signal cascade in lecture one and the NF-κB amplification loop in lecture five — what is this enzyme called?
questions.why: PKC is a signalling enzyme that can switch on inflammatory and growth pathways; he lists the 'detailed signal cascade' as content not to be memorised, but the starting point and the direction of the cascade have to be recognised.

questions.q: One of the DNA adducts formed by benzo(a)pyrene; he never asks you to memorise this abbreviation, but he explains the chain 'adduct → replication error → fixed as a mutation' very clearly — what is this adduct called?
questions.why: POB-DNA is one of the DNA adducts formed by benzo(a)pyrene; he did not ask you to memorise the abbreviation, so it is conceptual understanding, but he explains the chain 'adduct → replication error → fixed as a mutation' very clearly.

questions.q: Relaxed circular DNA, the relaxed circular DNA present before HBV enters the nucleus; he drew HBV's full life cycle on slide 17 — what is this DNA form called?
questions.why: rcDNA is relaxed circular DNA, the relaxed circular DNA present before HBV enters the nucleus; he did not single it out as a question in its own right, and he drew HBV's full life cycle on slide 17.

questions.q: He places this at the modern frontier of 'control of gene expression': delivering mRNA so that the patient's own ribosomes make the antigen, with the point being that the whole chain can be told using the central dogma — the instructions in DNA can be turned directly into a drug. What is such a vaccine called?
questions.why: An RNA vaccine delivers mRNA so that the patient's own ribosomes make the antigen; he does not ask you to memorise the chemistry of lipid nanoparticles — the point is that the whole chain can be told with the central dogma, that the instructions in DNA can be turned directly into a drug.

questions.q: This list in lecture two is itself teaching content. Why is CAR-T so ineffective in solid tumours, if the main reason is not that the CAR recognises the wrong cell?
options: Because solid tumours present all kinds of obstacles that disable CAR-T, such as the absence of chemokine receptors, the CD47 'do not eat me' signal and an immunosuppressive matrix
Because the CAR recognises the antigen of normal cells and cannot recognise the tumour
Because CAR-NK and CAR-macrophages take the targets away from CAR-T
Because solid tumours have no antigen to present
questions.why: The solid-tumour barriers are all the obstacles that make CAR-T fail in solid tumours, and this list is itself the teaching content of the passage; the missing receptors CCR2b and CCR4, CD47, CD73 and the matrix are all on it, and he does not ask you to memorise the names of the individual molecules on the list.

questions.q: Carcinogenic precursors specific to cigarettes; they are not directly carcinogenic themselves and only become electrophilic intermediates able to react with DNA after activation by liver P450 — what is this class of substances called?
questions.why: Tobacco-specific nitrosamines are the carcinogenic precursors specific to cigarettes; he does not ask you to memorise a list of carcinogens — what he asks you to remember is the causal chain from adduct to mutation.

questions.q: Background knowledge, not appearing in the content of the five lectures: a neuropeptide that can switch T cells off and thereby help the tumour hide — what is this neuropeptide called?
questions.why: VIP (vasoactive intestinal peptide) is a neuropeptide that can switch T cells off and help the tumour hide, and it is background knowledge; he did not list it as a question, and the VIP > 1.0 on the lecture-one metabolomics slide is variable importance in projection, which has nothing to do with this neuropeptide.

questions.q: An inheritance pattern carried on the X chromosome that appears in every generation; he discusses pedigree reading in both lecture two and lecture four, and the pedigree is one of the two big classes of scenario questions he names explicitly — what is this pattern called?
questions.why: X-linked dominant is the inheritance pattern carried on the X chromosome that appears in every generation; he discusses pedigree reading in both lecture two and lecture four, and the pedigree is indeed one of the two big classes of scenario questions he names explicitly (the other being survival curves).

questions.q: In lecture two, slide 29 sets X-linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial inheritance side by side, and he adds a special reminder: mitochondrial disease does not necessarily come from mtDNA. Why can you not draw a conclusion from the shape of a pedigree alone?
options: Because nuclear gene mutations can produce the same phenotype but a completely different inheritance pattern, so the answer has to mention both
Because X-linked recessive only affects women
Because mitochondrial DNA is inherited from the father
Because a pedigree can only identify autosomal disease
questions.why: X-linked recessive is the inheritance pattern carried on the X chromosome that mainly affects males; what he particularly wants you to remember is that easily-missed reminder: mitochondrial disease does not necessarily come from mtDNA, because nuclear gene mutations can produce the same phenotype with a completely different inheritance pattern, so the answer has to mention both.
